Spanish Literature. The body of written works produced in Spain and Spanish-speaking regions, encompassing some of Europe's most influential and distinctive voices. The tradition is founded on a unique blend of Christian, Jewish, and Islamic traditions due to Spain's medieval history of religious coexistence and conflict, reaching back to the medieval Reconquista.

The Spanish Golden Age, known as the Siglo de Oro, spanned the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries and was a peak of literary, artistic, and cultural achievement rivaling Italy's Renaissance. Miguel de Cervantes and his novel Don Quixote, published in sixteen oh-five, is often called the first modern novel. It revolutionized narrative form across Europe and defined the entire tradition of Spanish letters. Lope de Vega was the most prolific dramatist of the Golden Age, inventing Spanish theatrical conventions that influenced European drama fundamentally.

In the twentieth century, the Generation of ninety-eight responded to Spain's loss of empire, producing philosophers and writers like Miguel de Unamuno who grappled with national identity. Federico García Lorca brought modern Spanish poetry to international acclaim before his execution in the Spanish Civil War, and his work brought the tradition into the contemporary era. Spanish literature uniquely bridges European intellectual traditions and the literatures of Latin America, making it a global cultural hub whose influence extends far beyond Spain's borders.
